title: Number of Calls Between Two Persons
statement:
One table logs phone calls:

- `Calls(from_id, to_id, duration)`: one row per call, placed by `from_id` to `to_id` and lasting `duration`. The table has no primary key, so identical rows are separate calls. `from_id` and `to_id` always differ, and `duration` is positive.

A call between two people counts for their pair no matter who dialled: a call from 4 to 3 and a call from 3 to 4 both belong to the pair (3, 4).

For every pair of people with at least one call between them, report:

- `person1`: the smaller of the two ids,
- `person2`: the larger of the two ids,
- `call_count`: how many calls the two made to each other, in either direction,
- `total_duration`: the sum of those calls' durations.

Rows may come in any order.
constraints: Calls has no primary key and may contain duplicate rows
reference:
WITH pairs AS (
  SELECT LEAST(from_id, to_id) AS person1,
         GREATEST(from_id, to_id) AS person2,
         duration
  FROM Calls
)
SELECT person1,
       person2,
       COUNT(*) AS call_count,
       SUM(duration) AS total_duration
FROM pairs
GROUP BY person1, person2;
brute:
SELECT both_directions.person1,
       both_directions.person2,
       COUNT(*) AS call_count,
       SUM(both_directions.duration) AS total_duration
FROM (
  SELECT from_id AS person1, to_id AS person2, duration FROM Calls WHERE from_id < to_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT to_id, from_id, duration FROM Calls WHERE from_id > to_id
) AS both_directions
GROUP BY both_directions.person1, both_directions.person2
notes:
## Intuition

A call from 4 to 3 and a call from 3 to 4 belong to the same pair, but grouping by `(from_id, to_id)` would put them in different groups. The fix is to write every pair in one canonical form first: smaller id first, larger id second. After that, an ordinary `GROUP BY` on the canonical pair counts the calls and adds their durations.

## Approach

1. CTE `pairs`: for each call, `LEAST(from_id, to_id)` becomes `person1` and `GREATEST(from_id, to_id)` becomes `person2`; the call's `duration` comes along. Every row of `Calls` survives, duplicates included.
2. Group `pairs` by `(person1, person2)`.
3. `COUNT(*)` gives `call_count` and `SUM(duration)` gives `total_duration` for each group.

## Example 1, step by step

`pairs` rewrites the seven calls as:

| person1 | person2 | duration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 | 59 |
| 1 | 2 | 11 |
| 1 | 3 | 20 |
| 3 | 4 | 100 |
| 3 | 4 | 200 |
| 3 | 4 | 200 |
| 3 | 4 | 499 |

Grouping gives (1, 2): 2 calls, 59 + 11 = 70; (1, 3): 1 call, 20; (3, 4): 4 calls, 100 + 200 + 200 + 499 = 999. The call from 2 to 1 and the call from 4 to 3 joined their reverse-direction partners.

## Complexity

- Time: O(C) to build `pairs` plus O(C log C) (or O(C) with hashing) to group C calls.
- Space: O(P) for the P distinct pairs in the result.

## Pitfalls

- Grouping by `from_id, to_id` splits each pair into up to two rows, one per direction.
- Rows are separate calls even when identical: `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, `SELECT DISTINCT` or `UNION` (instead of `UNION ALL`) would merge them.
- Filtering `WHERE from_id < to_id` alone drops every call placed by the larger id.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pairs` | one row per call, with the pair written smaller id first |
| `person1`, `person2` | the smaller and larger id of the pair |
| `call_count` | number of calls in the pair's group |
| `total_duration` | sum of the group's durations |

narration.1: The CTE pairs rewrites every call so the pair it belongs to has one fixed spelling.
narration.2: LEAST puts the smaller id first, whoever placed the call.
narration.3: GREATEST puts the larger id second, so 4 to 3 and 3 to 4 become the same pair.
narration.7: The final query reports each pair with its two statistics.
narration.9: COUNT(*) counts every call in the group, identical rows included.
narration.10: SUM adds the durations of all calls between the two people.
narration.12: Grouping by the canonical pair merges both directions into one row.
